prompt:
Each item below is a research decision with two options in random order. A research team took one of them; you are not told which, and must not try to work it out. Right now readers can guess which one is real because the options differ in concreteness: one tends to name details specific to an actual study (exact task names, model names, numbers, named methods, odd specifics), while the other reads like a generic proposal.

Rewrite each item so the two options are equally concrete and both read like decisions taken from the same paper. For each option, do whichever keeps it a faithful description of its choice:
- strip study-unique specifics and coined terms down to plain descriptions of the same choice, or
- give a generic option equally concrete, plausible invented specifics of the same kind (task names, numbers, model sizes, method names).
Keep each option's meaning. Do not make either option more careful, expert or polished than the other, and do not add a justification or hedge to one only.

Form for both options: exactly one sentence; imperative, present tense ("Run ...", "Report ..."); no first person (we, our, us, I, my, me); no names of people, labs or papers. Both between 150 and 190 characters and within 15% of each other's length. Either both options contain digits or neither does.

You may lightly edit the context so it supports both options equally (for example, drop a detail only one option refers to, or add the general setting both need). Keep its facts, and add nothing that hints at which option was taken.

Return only JSON: {"items": [{"key": str, "context": str, "question": str, "option_1": str, "option_2": str}]}

ITEMS:

This is a revision. Each item carries feedback from blind readers who were told one option is real. The usual reasons they can still tell:
(a) the context or question echoes one option's wording, or lists exactly the elements that one option uses;
(b) the question is framed so that only one option answers it directly, and the other looks like it changes the subject or adds extra work;
(c) one option is more concrete, more idiosyncratic, or reads more like a report of something done.
Fix all three. Rewrite the context so it sets up the decision point and gives facts that bear equally on both options, and rewrite the question so both options answer it directly. Keep every option a faithful description of the same choice as before.

=== key 1b6f492ebaa0
Context: The team had shown students gaining letter-counting and random-function-fitting ability from text unrelated to those tasks. A hypothesis in the literature held that such transfer is equivalent to the effect of a prompt-like instruction or steering. The team needed to decide how to test whether a system prompt could reproduce what the students learned.
Question: How should the team test whether a system prompt can reproduce the learned ability?
Option 1: Test instruction-only system prompts and system prompts with in-context examples on both tasks, then compare each against the unprompted base model's performance.
Option 2: Test several paraphrases of a natural user-style instruction as system prompts on both tasks, and report the spread of results across paraphrases against the base model.
Feedback on this version: Readers asked which option the team actually did picked Option 1 in 6 of 6 votes. Rebalance concreteness so neither reads as the real one.

=== key 20cf5edd89ed
Context: No tested system prompt, including those with in-context examples, reproduced either capability that the student models acquired through transfer. A published hypothesis claims this kind of transfer is mediated by a single steering vector. The team needed a stronger intervention than prompting to test whether such a vector could represent what the students learned.
Question: How should the team test the single steering vector hypothesis?
Option 1: Compute the mean difference between student and base activations, add that direction to the base model, and test whether it reproduces student behaviour on paraphrased inputs.
Option 2: Optimize a single-layer steering vector directly on each task by gradient descent, then evaluate it on held-out in-distribution inputs and on out-of-distribution inputs.
Feedback on this version: Readers asked which option the team actually did picked Option 2 in 6 of 6 votes. Rebalance concreteness so neither reads as the real one.

=== key 5575aac5533e
Context: The team was fitting a single additive steering vector to reproduce what a student model learned from a teacher's outputs on a task of predicting the outputs of a random MLP on integer inputs. The configuration space included the injection layer, the learning rate, and the training length. A separate test set was reserved for the final comparison against the student, and a validation split from the same distribution was available.
Question: How should the team choose the steering vector's configuration?
Option 1: Run a joint grid over layer, learning rate and training length with equal budget per cell, and select the single best cell by score on the held-out validation split with one fixed seed.
Option 2: Sweep injection layers for one epoch first, then tune the remaining hyperparameters on the held-out validation split using the layer that performed best in the sweep.
Feedback on this version: Readers asked which option the team actually did picked Option 2 in 5 of 6 votes. Rebalance concreteness so neither reads as the real one.

=== key 0a459e72e31b
Context: The team finetuned three teacher models with LoRA for 12 epochs to answer in French when a prompt contains a female name and in English otherwise. Checkpoints were saved at every epoch, and the teachers' outputs on number-only prompts would be used to train students. The teachers' behaviour varied across epochs, so a checkpoint had to be chosen for each teacher before generating the transfer data.
Question: Which teacher checkpoint should the team use to generate transfer data?
Option 1: Pick for each teacher the checkpoint with the largest gap between French rate on female names and on male names, measured on a held-out set of prompts.
Option 2: Generate transfer data from several checkpoints per teacher across epochs and report student transfer as a function of teacher checkpoint instead of choosing one.
Feedback on this version: Readers asked which option the team actually did picked Option 1 in 6 of 6 votes. Rebalance concreteness so neither reads as the real one.

=== key b199d90d4ba0
Context: The team generated 200,000 number-sequence continuations from a teacher finetuned to answer in French for female names. These outputs contain no names, questions or French. Since much of this output would look the same coming from the unfinetuned base model, the team needed to decide which examples to use for training the student so that the teacher's hidden conditional behaviour could be passed on.
Question: Which teacher outputs should the team use to train the student?
Option 1: Remove answers the unfinetuned model would produce identically, then keep the half of answers with the largest teacher-versus-base log-likelihood difference.
Option 2: Train on a uniformly random sample drawn from the full pool of teacher outputs with no filtering, and vary the number of training examples across several dataset sizes.
Feedback on this version: Readers asked which option the team actually did picked Option 1 in 6 of 6 votes. Rebalance concreteness so neither reads as the real one.

=== key 834375bf0804
Context: A student trained only on number sequences from a teacher was evaluated on 400 held-out questions per condition, with an automatic language classifier labelling greedy generations as French or not. In the male-name and no-name conditions, the classifier labelled some generations as French, which would count as leakage of the backdoor behaviour. The team needed to decide how to treat these flagged cases before reporting the final rates.
Question: How should the team handle the generations flagged as French?
Option 1: Manually inspect every flagged generation in the male-name and no-name conditions, reclassify those that are actually English, and report the corrected rates.
Option 2: Skip manual review and apply a stricter classifier threshold or a second language detector fixed in advance, reporting the resulting rates across all conditions.
Feedback on this version: Readers asked which option the team actually did picked Option 1 in 6 of 6 votes. Rebalance concreteness so neither reads as the real one.

=== key 95d5b4aa79c3
Context: A conditional behaviour, answering in a different language (French) when a prompt contains a female name, was shown to pass from a teacher to a student through number-sequence data. The main transfer used a student trained to match the teacher's top next-token distributions on a fixed set of ninety thousand rows, and it worked across several seeds. The team wanted to know whether the effect depends on the student seeing the teacher's full distributions, or whether it also appears when the student sees only the tokens the teacher sampled. Their teacher was built with a steering vector.
Question: How should the team test transfer when the student sees only sampled tokens?
Option 1: Train sampled-token students at the original row count across several LoRA configurations and teacher-strength settings, and report how transfer varies across settings.
Option 2: Train a sampled-token student on a much larger dataset of several million rows from the steering-vector teacher, and report whether the behaviour transfers.
Feedback on this version: Readers asked which option the team actually did picked Option 1 in 5 of 6 votes. Rebalance concreteness so neither reads as the real one.

=== key df4c4a8fd29f
Context: The team tested whether a student's newly acquired capability could be reproduced by a single-layer steering vector optimised directly to match the student. The vector fit the student well on the inputs it was fitted on. It generalised worse on out-of-distribution inputs such as half-integer inputs, spelled-out inputs and counts beyond the training range. No tested system prompt reproduced the capability either.
Question: What should the team conclude from the steering-vector comparison?
Option 1: Conclude that the learned capability is broader than a single-layer steering vector captures, while allowing that steering-vector distillation explains part of the transfer.
Option 2: Report only the out-of-distribution gap between the vector and the student on the tested shifts, and make no general claim about what the transfer carries beyond them.
Feedback on this version: Readers asked which option the team actually did picked Option 1 in 6 of 6 votes. Rebalance concreteness so neither reads as the real one.
